article_text:
M useums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as the new design museum in Ghent . Rising above the Belgian city’s medieval tiled rooftops like an angular white watchtower, the new building has vacuumed up the city’s condemned concrete frames, windows, car windscreens, sinks and old toilets, and transformed them, phoenix-like, into a gleaming monument to recycling.

“There’s nothing new about reuse,” says Andy Groarke, co-founder of Carmody Groarke , the London-based architects who designed the €20m (£17m) project with local firms Atama and Re-st . “We’ve just forgotten how to do it.”

He says the team drew inspiration from Ghent’s 16th-century gothic cathedral, Saint Bavo’s, which was partly built using the white limestone blocks of the 10th-century romanesque basilica that had stood on the same site (recent renovations also ghoulishly uncovered walls made of human bones , femurs and tibias apparently having particularly useful structural properties, with crushed skulls for infill).

The new design museum doesn’t quite go that far in its nose-to-tail approach, but almost. The toilet cubicles are a smorgasbord of “biomaterials”, each featuring different tiles made of seaweed, flax, wood terrazzo and volcanic ash (you can scan a QR code for more info while you’re sitting on the loo). Some walls are plastered with local clay, while a chunky column in the entrance hall revels in its earthy layers of rubble dug straight from the building site.

But the real innovation is the brick , which was specially developed, tested and certified for the project (funded by a grant from Circular Flanders and Sogent, the city’s development agency). Each brick is made of 63% construction waste, sourced from within 8km of the museum, pulverised and compressed with hydrated lime, saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick. And the lime will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere as it cures over the coming months and years.

“We’re not claiming this is a panacea, or a solution to the climate crisis,” says architect Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different, with the right collaborators and the right clients.” Developed by East Sussex firm Local Works Studio and Brussels group BC Materials , the bricks were made in a former railway depot nearby, with the public invited to mix the ingredients and press their own blocks during a two-day festival of brickmaking. For €10, you can take one home from the museum shop.

Public participation extended to defining the very essence of the museum, too. In keeping with Belgium’s democratic traditions, a “citizens’ panel” of 40 people, drawn from a wide variety of Ghent residents, was established to inform what the museum should be. Their 100+ recommendations ranged from incorporating unticketed areas, to being able to see work-in-progress, and having plenty of seating, as well as ensuring that the “chic” building didn’t put people off. The result is as locally sourced and collaboratively created as big civic buildings come. “This expansion and renovation are not about creating more museum,” says the outgoing director, Katrien Laporte, “but about creating more than a museum: a community sense-making museum with real social relevance.”

The extension fills a leftover plot on the museum’s site, uniting the galleries that were previously spread between an 18th-century rococo mansion, called the Hotel de Coninck, and a troublesome 1990s addition – designed with a moving glass floor that rarely moved, now thankfully banished. The new building stands with the presence of a grand Ghent house, rising in five large storeys, and turning as it climbs to face the city centre, with big picture windows looking out in different directions on each floor. “We wanted it to feel domestic, industrial and civic at once,” says Groarke. It certainly has a bold presence.

Not everyone has welcomed its industrial bulk. Concerns have been raised about how the boxy white mass lumbers into view from the city’s quaint historical centre, and there is something slightly clumsy about the form on the skyline, topped with multiple roofs angled in different directions. Silicone joints between stretches of brick don’t help either, reading as unsightly seams from a distance. The museum defended the height as providing never-before-seen views of the city, and it’s true: when you’re on the top floor – a freely accessible public loft – or the roof terrace below, the panoramic vistas of Ghent’s castle and church spires are a treat.

Skyline concerns also fade away as you approach the museum at street level. A gate in the form of a billowing metallic curtain , frozen in motion, signals the new entrance in a delightfully surreal touch. Designed by Antwerp studio Unfold and 3D-printed in aluminium, it is a welcome change from the previously off-putting carriage entrance of the historical hotel down the sidestreet. The striking gate is one of a series of special projects commissioned by curator Siegrid Demyttenaere that have been dotted throughout the building, from a cast street number to a reception desk and lockers, making functional parts of the museum exhibits in themselves.

A lobby lined with timber salvaged from a tobacco factory in Brussels leads into the stadskamer , or city room, opening through big sliding windows on to the museum courtyard on one side, and the street on the other. It was thronging with visitors during the opening weekend, with the feeling of a true public square. The chubby earthen column (a commission by Grond Studio ) rises to support an intersection of the deep wooden beams that crisscross the ceiling, the first glimpse of the building’s sculptural timber frame. The architects say it is the biggest mass timber public building in Belgium, featuring walls and floors of spruce CLT (cross-laminated timber) and chunky beams of beech LVL (laminated veneer lumber), imported from Austria. A beautiful oak staircase connects the floors, with joinery details in darker walnut, its angular geometries lending a Piranesian air.

The new building is “a stack of five rooms”, says Groarke, “each with a particular identity”. The stairs lead to the Forum, for lectures and events; the Atelier, a light-flooded studio for education workshops; and the Vitrine for temporary exhibitions – before arriving at the Loft, a grand event space with spectacular views. Its balcony became an urban-scale DJ booth for the opening party, when local duo 2manydjs performed above the rooftops to 5,000 revellers dancing in the streets below.

Spectacle aside, one of the building’s most useful achievements is connecting the museum’s pre-existing wings in a continuous, accessible loop for the first time. Visitors can now move from the chandelier-bedecked suites of the Hotel de Coninck, through to the 90s wing – from which 60% of the columns have been removed and voids filled in to create more display space for the permanent collection – to the light, woody world of the new tower. It was made possible by a wise use of funds: while competing architects proposed taller towers and deeper basement levels, the winning team suggested a better use of some of the tight budget would be to refurbish and renew what was already there.

“The competition was such a great process,” says Groarke, singing the praises of the renowned Flemish Open Call run by the Vlaams Bouwmeester (the government architect), with a jury that included five international museum directors alongside architects and planners. You can still see all the entries online . “Architecture is in the public consciousness here in a way that it’s not in the UK,” Groarke continues. “Back home, it’s seen as an extension of the property industry, with a pyramid scheme of mediocrity in the way.”

He’s got a point. It would be hard to imagine a building of such quality and imagination being realised on British shores, where contractors rule all and architects are forced to compete on fees in a self-sabotaging race to the bottom. Public procurement rules also mean architects generally have to have built several buildings of the type they are bidding for before they can even qualify to compete, meaning few opportunities for young practices.

Our bureaucrats might do well to spend some time in the museum’s opening exhibition, Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy . Curated by Amelie Klein and Vera Sacchetti, it is a fascinating exploration of the design of democratic decision-making, examining everything from ballot papers to the layout of parliament buildings, to how nature might be given a seat at the table. One particularly revealing project, The Flemish Scrollers by artist Dries Depoorter, uses AI to track distracted politicians scrolling on their phones during parliamentary sessions, and automatically posts screenshots of the live stream to social media, asking the elected officials to do better.

Perhaps a similar algorithm could be used to name and shame each time a public tender is awarded to the same old suspects, with dismal results for our built environment. Once again, the Flems are leading the way.

article_text:
Pattern is presented as the first book devoted to a Mauritanian studio photographer: Amadou Fall, who portrayed the people of Nouadhibou at his Studio Grand Fall from the 1960s onward.

By Gaia Squarci. Photographs by Amadou Fall

“Pushing open the door of Studio Grand Fall meant leaving the street behind. The dust stayed outside. The noise too,” writes photographer Adrien Tache. Amadou Fall’s son entrusted Tache with bringing the archive to life, after decades of leaving it untouched. Nomadic families, city dwellers, Spanish migrants, merchants and officials all sat in front of his lens. Together they form a collective portrait of an Atlantic port where North Africa, West Africa and Europe met.

The clothes in Fall’s portraits tell that same story. For a long time, Mauritanian dress favoured plain or indigo-dyed cottons. Then came wax prints: cottons whose bold, colourful patterns are created by using wax to resist the dye. Dutch and British factories first produced them in imitation of Indonesian batik, intending to sell them in Asia. It was in West Africa, however, that they found their public during the nineteenth century, as traders and their customers gave each motif a name of their own, linked to marriage, wealth, migration or independence.

Rather than replacing traditional garments, wax cloth was integrated into existing ways of dressing, and by the 1960s it had become a sign of modernity and aspiration. That same cloth now binds the book: each copy is covered in a different wax fabric printed in West Africa, echoing the patterns some of the sitters could have been wearing.

The book Pattern is published by Fraglich Publishing and available for 35 Euro.

article_text:
Jenny Wu speaks to various nonprofits about fundraising and the types of compromises that may come with it

In May I was given a press ticket to a fundraising luncheon on Park Avenue. The main event was a talk between a painter of florid mixed-media tableaux represented by a blue-chip gallery and a curator from a major contemporary art institution. Onstage the artist expressed her love for New York, a place where, in her words, you could be enjoying a day out with friends one moment, and the next be startled by a furry little creature scampering across the sidewalk. Her quip made the audience chuckle, but what struck me was the way she could invoke – in one deft stroke – the filth and neglect that so many New Yorkers confront daily without so much as pointing a finger or uttering the word ‘rat’.

Making art about rats is another story. Art that, say, lets you watch them sniff around and climb on tiny sculptures installed near their habitats through night-vision-equipped trail cams. This is the premise of Asad Raza’s exhibition Thigmotaxis (the rat show) , on view through December in Times, an experimental, noncommercial art space that opened in February. “The rat show has been in the works between me and Asad for a few years,” Summer Guthery, one of Times’s two cofounders and previously the director of the arts nonprofit (and former exhibition space) Canal Projects, tells me over the phone. “I wanted to do it at Canal Projects, [but] something about rats just didn’t appeal to them.” Alongside cofounder Francesca Sonara, Guthery has been knee-deep in rat-related fieldwork with Raza for the past nine months. “Rats are not the problem. We are the problem,” Sonara says (Indeed, we dig up their burrows with construction equipment in the process of gentrifying neighbourhoods; we leave garbage bags out on the curb and are surprised to find them scavenging inside.) “Rats are gross because we’re gross.”

Times, which is based in a rented gallery space between Chinatown and Tribeca, opened seven months ago with a performance by Latvian choreographer Jana Jacuka that began as a standup comedy set and evolved into an opera and an exorcism (by the end, there was drool on the floor). Performances, exhibitions and screenings have followed, by Nina Beier, Bob Kil, Calla Henkel and Max Pitegoff, Liv Schulman and others. Guthery and Sonara are longtime friends and collaborators. “We have the same taste,” Guthery says. “We like the same weird shit.”

They are able to broadcast their taste unabashedly thanks to their arrangement: Sonara seed-funded Times, and while she and Guthery have since brought in other private donors, the two remain in full control of the programming. While other arts nonprofits – say, more robustly financed but also relatively new entities in the city such as Center for Art Research and Alliances (CARA) – tend to structure their governing bodies with discrete roles for the board, the founder, the executive director and so on, Sonara and Guthery pride themselves on handling daily operations together and working in equal partnership. They are, after all, the only members of Times’s board and, save for the occasional university-funded intern, Times’s only employees. Moreover, they’ve set up Times under what they call a ‘three-year obsolescence model’. Planned obsolescence – the promise for their nonprofit to essentially self-liquidate, so as not to bloat and ossify – is liberating, according to Sonara, because it allows them to focus “a comparatively smaller amount of money” on “a smaller period of time”, to avoid making artists perform a song and dance for the donor class. Of course, Guthery and Sonara can take this position because, at Times’s scale and given what will be its eternal youth, the duo can afford to be a bit cheeky.

A more typical, cautious model presents itself in nonprofits such as Triple Canopy, an online publishing platform devoted to experimental art and literature, which began as a nonhierarchical, unpaid editorial collective and became a 501(c)(3) – which is to say, a formal magazine with a compensated masthead – in 2010. Since its inception, Triple Canopy has sought to operate well beyond the standard purview of a magazine and has ‘published’ artworks, performances, lectures, workshops and even their own installation of reproductions of early American furniture and ‘primitive’ paintings in the 2014 Whitney Biennial. Last fall, artist Louis Osmosis kicked off the magazine’s annual interdisciplinary symposium with a performance during which he crawled on all fours and used chalk to number the holes in the floorboards of the auditorium, as if taking inventory for the vermin.

Today, Triple Canopy operates on a budget of approximately $1 million per year, their director Molly Kleiman tells me. Their work is heavily reliant on philanthropic giving: around 80 percent of their income is contributed, 60 percent from private foundations, the city and the state (they do not receive any federal government support), 20 percent from board members and individuals. Historically, the organisation has had, in Kleiman’s words, “very little cash buffer”. “We are fundraising for the year that we are currently in every year,” she says. In terms of their expenses, the organisation must pay rent on their office in Chinatown and pay its editors and designers. Kleiman observes that organisations often fare better when fundraising for new activities or a capital campaign than for existing programmes. “You have to smuggle funding your general operations into new initiatives in creative ways,” she says. “It’s something that we’re all doing all the time.” Conversely, one can choose not to perform for funders – or specifically not for certain funders whose values and politics are suspect – even if this refusal means “you stay smaller”, Kleiman said in June, speaking at To Build and Sustain, a conference in Montreal for independent arts publishers organised by Momus magazine, stressing, “Access to more funds always comes with different compromises.”

“We are in a much more stable position than we have been in the past,” Kleiman tells me, “due to a few multiyear grants from foundations that have been genuine partners of ours.” These include, among others, the Lambent Foundation: in 2024, with the foundation’s support, Triple Canopy began awarding fellowships to genre-bending, public-spirited artists such as Jeremy Toussaint-Baptiste, Alex Tatarsky and New Red Order. Kleiman emphasises that the Lambent Foundation’s executive director, Michelle Coffey, convenes with grantees in closed-door sessions during which they share with one another the operational challenges they face. This type of procedure provides relief because grantees are able to converse rather than compete; they are also spared the awkwardness of describing everything they’ve done as a success to the funder – even the endeavours that fail – and having to then repeat the same ‘successful’ strategies year after year.

It’s not that weird and worthwhile programming does not take place at larger nonprofits like CARA, which occupies a nearly $17m property in the West Village purchased by Jane Hait, stepdaughter of billionaire Howard Marks. I have fond memories of dancers choreographed by Ligia Lewis slouched against the walls of that building. But there is often a palpable disconnect between the progressive, experimental ethos these types of entities profess and their pseudo-corporate governance structures, which affect increasing numbers of people as the organisations grow in age and ambition.

CARA, an exhibition space and supporter of arts-related research and publication that opened in 2022, is currently governed by 13 independent voting members plus Hait, serving as founder and board chair, and curator Manuela Moscoso, acting as executive and artistic director. There is still work to be done, Moscoso tells me over email, to clarify how the board and management make decisions and hold one another accountable. Internal improvements are made via cycles of audits, and Hait informs me that “there simply aren’t enough hours in the day to do it all”. Relatedly, burnout is a real risk among employees working to execute the vision of what Hait calls “a board with big dreams”, which involve, according to Moscoso, “evolv[ing] from a founder-initiated project into a public institution” and “making what we have built durable”. But Hait tells me CARA must continue to grow, because, as it stands, the number of good artists still exceeds the artworld’s capacity to care for their practices and legacies. Growth means anything from increasing funding and staff in order to expand their fellowship programme, which currently offers two $75,000 awards every two years, to publishing more books so as to reach a wider public.

All the while staying conscious of the fact that, in Moscoso’s words, “an institution can grow in size while becoming thinner in purpose”. The question is whether any organisation can truly buck the trend, and until that happens, it might behove us to pay attention to the ones scurrying past our feet, pursuing models that are smaller, ever nimbler and more terranean, with noses and ears to the ground.

article_text:
「百姓のため」といいつつ本当の狙いは……

大河ドラマ「豊臣兄弟！」第43回はそのタイトル通り、秀吉（池松壮亮さん）の施策として特に名高い「刀狩り」をテーマに据えました。九州を平定し、天下一統にほぼ目途が立った天正16年（1588）7月、秀吉は３か条からなる刀狩令を発布しました。

以下のような内容でした。

①諸国の百姓の刀、脇差、弓、槍、鉄砲、その他武具の類いの所持を堅く禁じる。不要の武具を貯え、一揆を企てればやがてその身を滅ぼすことになる。 ②没収した武具は無駄にせず、これを鋳潰して大仏建立のための釘や 鎹 にする。これによって百姓たちは来世までも救われるだろう。 ③百姓たちは耕作に専念するすれば子々孫々に至るまで安穏長久である。百姓たちに同情するからこそ、このように命じるのだ。

社会の安定のためには不可避の武力統制

ーーという趣旨でした。百姓の安寧な暮らしを願うからこそ、という立て付けにはなっていますが、その主眼はやはり一揆の防止だったでしょう。日本の歴史を振り返ってみても、刀狩りに類似した施策は古くは鎌倉時代にも行われ、戦国時代でも各地の大名が試みており、この時期に近接した例では柴田勝家が越前で武器の没収を行っていました。為政者として、武力の統制は社会の安定と治安の向上のために避けて通れない道ですが、百姓ら庶民にとっても、依然として動乱の時代が続いているという現実があり、自衛などのため簡単に武器を手放せるものではないことはドラマでも描かれていたとおりです。

板挟みの諸大名も苦慮

刀狩りの実行を求められた諸大名も苦労しました。薩摩の島津家ではこの時期、各国で徴収された武器が京都に集められる中、島津領内の刀を献上することができず、領主らが心配している、という書状が残されています。ぼやぼやしていて、国元で一揆が起ころうものなら、領内の治安を守れず切腹を命じられた佐々成政（白洲迅さん）の二の舞になりかねません。かといって地域の実情を把握していれば、刀狩りが容易ではないことも分かり切っていたことでしょう。

「新しい世なぞ誰も望んでいない」。「戦がなくなったら、手柄を立てる場もなくなる。恩賞に預かれない者たちはどうやって生きればよいのか」。佐々にそう言わせたシナリオは、秀吉らが導こうとしている新しい時代に適応したくてもできない、戦国時代を生きてきた人々の本音をむき出しに表現していました。

急激な時代の変化についていけず、もがき苦しんだり、反発したりする人の気持ちはいつの世も変わりません。AIの急激な発展などでこれまでの価値観が通用しなくなり、将来の社会像が見えにくくなっている私たちにとっても、他人事とは思えません。

斬り合いとなった場面で、佐々が秀長に「思えば、お前とは初めて会った時もこうして刃を交えたな」と言ったのは、第6回「兄弟の絆」のエピソードでした。 大沢次郎左衛門（松尾諭さん）を陥れる陰謀を見抜いた小一郎が、信長の命で大沢の持ち物に刃物を隠す工作を行った佐々を問い詰め、激しいつばぜり合いになりました。懐かしい場面が蘇りました。

北条も「反動」を期待

さて事実上、最後に残った秀吉に対する強力な抵抗勢力、関東の北条氏政（谷原章介さん）も「揺り戻し」に期待する向きでした。

「刀狩りのような無謀な策を進めれば、やがて各地で大名や民から不満が噴き出す。時を引き延ばすのだ。そうすれば秀吉は自ずと崩れ落ちる」。危ういバランスの中で秀吉と秀長の兄弟は新政策を遂行できるのでしょうか。

最良のアドバイザー、利休

ここで登場したのが千利休（吉岡秀隆さん）です。今や圧倒的な権力の高みに立ち、世間の実情から疎くなりがちな兄弟に絶妙なアドバイスを送ります。

利休は兄弟が推し進める政策を列挙していきました。

「検地」「惣無事」「伴天連の追放」「喧嘩停止」「海賊停止」そして今回の「刀狩り」です。それぞれになぞらえたお菓子が、積み上げるとあっという間に崩れ落ちてしまいました。

「惣無事」は大名間の武力の行使を禁止したもの。「喧嘩停止」は農民間の戦いを制限したこと。「海賊停止」は刀狩りを海の民にも拡張適用したものです。この時期、兄弟が社会の仕組みを大きく変える決まりを次々と広めてきたのが一目瞭然です。

利休、「短い間にようここまでおやりになりましたなあ」と感嘆しつつ、「無理に積み上げようとすれば、一瞬で潰れてしまうかも」。

「われらに不満を抱くものがおるのだな」。察しのいい秀長、利休のメッセージをしっかりと受け止めます。誰もが思わず心を開いてしまう茶室という密閉された環境の中で、魅力あふれる人柄の利休が様々な声を受け止めていたことを伺わせました。

得意の「芝居」で“五大老”の理解を得る

徳川家康、前田利家、毛利輝元、宇喜多秀家、小早川隆景という錚々たる顔ぶれを居城の大和郡山城に招待しました。秀長亡きあと、豊臣家を支えた「五大老」を揃えた形です。もしかしたら秀長は自分が亡きあとを想定していた？と、想像を逞しくしてしまう場面でもありました。

ドラマの場面はフィクションでしょうけれど、この時期、秀長が居城に有力大名を招いたのは史実通りです。天正16年4月、秀吉が京都の聚楽第に後陽成天皇を招いた「聚楽第行幸」の後のことです。続く7月に毛利輝元と一門衆の小早川隆景らが秀吉に拝謁するため上洛すると、秀長は彼らの案内役を務め、9月に聚楽第での秀吉との拝謁など京都で一連の行事が終わった後、わざわざ大和郡山城に寄ってもらい、接待しました。

諸大名との連携を密に取り、豊臣家との絆を深めるために汗をかいた秀長の姿が浮かび上がります。今回は旧知の家康（松下洸平さん）、利家（大東駿介さん）に一役買ってもらい、「秀吉は天下人の器ではない。俺が代わって関白になる」という大風呂敷を拡げ、得意の小芝居で秀吉に対する本音を聞き出そうとしました。途中でウソがばれ、腰砕けの展開になりましたが、それもすべて計算づくだったのかもしれません。

結果的に、秀長でさえ自分の領地で刀狩りを完全に行うのは難しい状況を見せることで、「刀狩り」をはじめとする秀吉の施策について、５人の有力者の不満や焦りを和らげることに成功したようです。筆作りの名人の才蔵（間宮祥太朗さん）が登場する事も含めて、全部が芝居でも不思議ではないのが秀長のしたたかなところです。

怒り渦巻く秀次

秀吉の命に沿って領内の刀狩りを厳格に実行し、武器を隠していた領民を厳罰にさえ処した秀次（山田涼介さん）は、秀長の中途半端なやり方を聞いて納得がいきません。「諸大名に示しがつかない」と批判します。しかし肝心の秀吉といえば、思わぬことを言い出します。

「一度や二度の令でうまくいくとは思っていない。何度もしくじりを繰り返しながら、武具などなくても生きていける世があるのだと、少しづつ民に分かってもらうことが大事。秀長は刀ではなく、民の心を絡めとったのだ。さすがわが弟」と絶賛です。

「自分は不本意でも殿下の沙汰を守り、刀狩りを実行したのに…」。同じ身内でもこの扱いの差、評価の差は何なのだろうか、と怒りが沸き上がる秀次でした。暗雲がさらに広がる豊臣家です。

（美術展ナビ編集班 岡部匡志）

As Laika debuts its latest stop-motion animation, Travis Knight is standing firmly against generative AI .

The Wildwood director and Laika CEO explained that GenAI “is antithetical to everything that we are at this studio,” also emphasizing that he hopes people “see the danger” in the technology’s potential as much as the “value.”

“But all of these things have meaning and value when you put them in the hands of an artist,” he told The Verge . “When the technology is doing the work of the artist, that’s a different proposition. And that’s something that I am steadfastly against, because there is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that.

Knight continued, “When you’ve ingested the material that an artist has actually created, and then regurgitate it in a different way, there’s no soul, there’s no spirit, there’s no humanity behind it. That’s theft.”

Watch on Deadline

While he conceded that “AI is extraordinary technology” that could reap great benefits in medicine and science and “benefit humanity tremendously,” he also sees “a world where they can be devastating.”

“I fear for the latter, I hope for the former, but it requires people to be good stewards of this technology,” he explained. “As a group of humans we have not shown generally that we’re good at that. But I’m ever an optimist, and I hope that collectively we can see the value in the technology and use it responsibly, and see the danger in the technology and push back against it.”

Knight’s comments come amid ongoing concerns around AI’s plagiarism of copyrighted materials and the threat it poses to jobs in Hollywood and beyond, as well as recent warnings from those working in AI that continued progress could “ cause a billion deaths .”

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order last month to fast-track stringent oversight and control of AI. Convening “a group of world-leading experts” within the next 60 days, the order lays out a discussion of “safety plans” and “an emergency shutoff, or ‘kill switch,’ for frontier models.”

On a federal level, Trump has brushed off concerns about AI as “a hoax,” insisting the U.S. government “already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI companies.

Book Review

The War on Art Is Repeating Itself

As an artist who lived through the Reagan-era Culture Wars, I recommend Isaac Butler’s “The Perfect Moment” for the stories that parallel our current fight to defend creative expression.

Washington Post via Getty Images, all images courtesy Bloomsbury)

Critic and theater director Isaac Butler is younger than I am, so he didn’t live through the Culture Wars of the Reagan ’80s. During this time, for instance, the Morality Action Committee wrote postcards to legislators across the country claiming that Franklin Furnace — the arts organization I founded 50 years ago — had shown pornography to 500 children per day during our Carnival Knowledge exhibition of women artists exploring sexuality. But as an art aficionado, he saw an alarming development in 2020, when an exhibition of Philip Guston’s work was postponed by the Tate Modern; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston; and the National Gallery of Art for fear that his paintings referencing the Ku Klux Klan might be misinterpreted by the public. In light of the current rise of right-wing legislators, politicians, and organizations targeting arts and culture in the United States, the parallel story of the conservative players of the 1980s and ’90s needs to be told.

Butler’s book, The Perfect Moment: God, Sex, Art, and the Birth of America's Culture Wars (2026), discusses major events in that tumultuous era of the 1980s and ’90s, including the difficulty Martin Scorsese had producing The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), primarily caused by Reverend Donald Wildmon’s innovation of mass mailing to Christians on behalf of his National Federation for Decency. Wildmon appears again in Butler’s discussion of Andres Serrano ’s infamous “Piss Christ” (1987), a photograph of a plastic crucifix in a beaker of the artist’s urine. In 1989, then-Senator Alfonse D’Amato ripped a reproduction of a catalog image of Serrano’s artwork in half on the Senate floor.

The Perfect Moment: God, Sex, Art, and the Birth of America's Culture Wars by Isaac Butler (Bloomsbury, 2026)

Then there’s the story that gives the book its name: the cancellation of The Perfect Moment, a Robert Mapplethorpe retrospective, by the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. By the mid-1980s, Mapplethorpe’s AIDS diagnosis had become common knowledge. Although The Perfect Moment had traveled nationally, its depiction of sadomasochism, Black nude models, and naked children was likely going to get a reaction in Washington. So on June 12, 1989, the Corcoran Gallery of Art decided to cancel the exhibition before it opened, after which Jesse Helms and Sidney Yates, a Democratic Congressman from Illinois, fought over the funding of the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) itself. Butler provides a balanced account of how both sides strategized and implemented their ambitions.
excerpt_original: As an artist who lived through the Reagan-era Culture Wars, I recommend Isaac Butler’s “The Perfect Moment” for the stories that parallel our current fight to defend creative expression.

article_text:
The artist approaches colour intuitively, using it as a means of experimentation, harmony and freedom in her practice.

Canvas: You trained as an architect before pursuing a career as an artist. What prompted that shift?

Radia Lamrani Karim: My mother is an architect, so I have always been surrounded by this world, and she taught me many things about architecture and art. I studied interior design and architecture in Paris and then went on to an internship in New York with Amale Andraos’s firm called WORKac. That’s when everything changed for me. I was spending a lot of time in museums and galleries and became passionate about art because I discovered how free artists are. This aspect really touched me. I grew up in Morocco, and as a woman, I had never experienced this kind of freedom before. I had always drawn since I was young, making drawings and creating things, but my parents would say, “Radia, study architecture. It is safer. It is more secure.” Then, during the pandemic, on the first day of lockdown, I don’t know why, but I just started painting and I have never stopped. I had been working as an architect in Paris for four years, but when I started having clients and developing projects with my art, I decided to leave my job and become a full-time artist.

How does your background in architecture continue to inform the way you approach your art?

Painting is often a direct relationship between the artist and the canvas, but architecture encourages you to consider things more globally. It teaches you structure, precision and attention to detail. I think this influence appears in my desire to create immersive experiences. I don’t only want people to look at my paintings,I want them to enter a different world.

Does colour play a role in how you see and experience the world?

I have always played with colours and I love textures, painting and different combinations. The way I use colour comes from my desire to experiment. I like showing people that unexpected combinations can work together. Sometimes people tell me, “I never imagined these colours could exist together” and I love that reaction. Maybe colour has also been a form of rebellion against the conformity I experienced growing up. There were many expectations about how a woman should behave and what she should become. Through colour, I found a way to express myself and show that being different can also be accepted.

When starting a work, how do you select your colour palette?

I experiment a lot. I might begin with one palette, but if I do not feel that the colours work together, I replace them until I find the I mix them with red, but if it’s not working then I might try pink instead. It is always a process of trial and error. I can spend three weeks working on one painting, even if people do not see all the layers and decisions behind the final result.

In works such as MÉDITERRANÉE (2025) and Within the Red Moon (2025), tiny dots accumulate to create vast landscape-like scenes. How do these different visual languages work together?

I always begin with drawings on paper. I usually start small because it is easier and faster, and then I project the drawing onto the painting. With the small pearls or dots, I am interested in creating volume and depth. I always try to bring something new because I do not like repeating the same thing. For me, art is about experimentation. I am always trying to discover new shapes, new ways of creating and new possibilities beyond the two-dimensional surface.

Earlier this year, you presented a site-specific installation as part of the second chapter of the group show Painting in the Exercise of Art at 1-54 Marrakech. Could you talk us through the process of creating the work?

Loft Art Gallery invited me to make a site-specific installation for the exhibition. I created Floating Mountains (2025). I wanted it to have the feeling of floating, almost as if the forms were suspended, with soft, wave-like shapes and different gradients of colour. The colours create a calming atmosphere, while the movement of the forms gives a sense of being surrounded and protected. I wanted people to experience a feeling of safety and immersion. It is connected to my paintings but transformed into a three-dimensional experience where people can walk around and engage with the work differently.

What are you currently working on?

I am developing a series entitled Every sunrise begins with new eyes (2023–). I started working on this three years ago, after leaving my job and searching for a new perspective. The title means that even if something feels difficult today, it can change tomorrow. You’re never permanently stuck in one situation. The series is about believing in possibilities and that you can create change in your life and move towards something better.

article_text:
Can AI help identify the sitters in historical portraits? This is the question pondered by an interdisciplinary project as well as an exhibition that opened this month at Geneva’s Musée d’art et d’histoire (MAH), showcasing a dozen 1762 chalk drawings of the family of Austria’s Empress Maria Theresa by the 18th-century artist Jean-Étienne Liotard .

Twenty years ago, when Catriona Seth was preparing to publish a book about Marie-Antoinette, she chose a beloved childhood portrait of the storied French queen by the 18th-century artist Jean-Étienne Liotard as the book’s cover illustration. Only years later, while researching the early life of this infamously decapitated royal, did she realize something wasn’t quite right. The young lady depicted in that chalk drawing has the chivalric medal of the Order of the Starry Cross pinned to her ruffled pink dress; Marie-Antoinette too received that medal but hadn’t yet in 1762 when Liotard (1702–1789) was in Vienna producing a series of portraits of the many children of Empress Maria Theresa of Austria.

As it turned out, the portrait that Seth used to illustrate the cover of her book wasn’t of Marie-Antoinette at all, as had long been believed, but rather of her sister Marie-Caroline.

“I love being able to say that to people, because it just shows that research is a continuous process and that we also learn by our mistakes,” says Seth, a French literature professor at All Souls College, University of Oxford. “There are things that can be discovered, even about great portraits, great texts. We have to think about them and question things.”

Seth had historical proof that the portrait formerly identified as Marie-Antoinette was of Marie-Caroline, but it was a trickier matter to claim the opposite: that the portrait once thought to be Marie-Caroline was actually of Marie-Antoinette. Remembering popular filters she’d seen online, Seth wondered what would happen if she uploaded the portrait into an app that ages faces by 10 or 20 years. She did so, and then compared the result to an adult portrait of the French reine . “It wasn’t very useful,” admits Seth. “But I thought: There’s an idea here.”

Seth mentioned this to Marie-Eve Celio-Scheurer, senior curator and head of the graphic arts department at Geneva’s Musée d’art et d’histoire (MAH), which holds the largest collection of Liotard portraits in the world (including the two in question). Celio-Scheurer in turn reached out to David-Olivier Jacquet-Chiffelle, a professor of forensic science and identification at the University of Lausanne, home to the world’s oldest school of forensic science. He connected with Sébastien Marcel, an expert in biometrics and face recognition.

Together, the team posed the question: Can modern AI and biometric technologies be used to identify people in centuries-old artistic portraits?

They’re attempting to answer this question through a joint experimental project, INTERART, which is a collaboration among the MAH, the University of Oxford, Idiap Research Institute, and the University of Lausanne’s School of Criminal Justice. Identifying a sitter in a portrait is a tricky art-historical task that involves a study of provenance, inscriptions, archival documentation, iconographic juxtaposition, collection history, and costume and jewelry. Could present-day technologies be another item in the researcher’s tool kit?

Results of the project, at this early stage, are part of an exhibition that opened this month at MAH titled Liotard & Marie-Antoinette: Faces Under Investigation , and an accompanying catalog. The show, on view through February 7, 2027, presents all 11 drawings of Marie-Therese’s children, plus one portrait of their father, François-Étienne de Lorraine, that recently entered the museum’s collection. In the exhibition, Liotard’s portraits of Marie-Antoinette and Marie Caroline have been newly titled to reflect the true identities of the sitters.

Current facial recognition systems, originally developed for photographs, can compare faces despite differences in pose, lighting, expression, age, and image quality. They were never intended to be used on paintings, where two portraits of the same sitter may have major differences in style and technique. The challenge, then, is to create models that can recognize facial constants regardless of changes introduced through artistic practice. One caveat: For a painting to be effectively analyzed through biometrics and AI, it needs to have been created directly before the sitter, and therefore truest to the person’s likeness (rather than a copy of an existing portrait, for example).

The potential of such a model would be to generate thresholds of probability, not provide conclusive answers. “There is never a 100 percent correct answer, and this is what also keeps the project interesting,” says Celio-Scheurer. “It gives you a potential.”

This path holds promise, but it needs refining. The algorithm can suggest associations that wouldn’t naturally occur to scholars and may help in the identification of people in portraits. “We all know museums are full of portraits of an unknown woman or an unknown man, that sort of thing, and if we can have databases of portraits where we know exactly who a sitter is, where we know exactly what their age was, we know they sat for the portrait, et cetera, then by putting an unidentified portrait into the mix, the algorithm can probably suggest things to us,” Seth explains. “It might give us leads.” In this sense, it would be a bit like a database of criminals, where you provide a suspect’s fingerprints and hope for a match.

Seth and Celio-Scheurer are careful to warn that these tools won’t replace the human eye or traditional research. Rather, they could be additional aids. “Art historians [are] quite curious about this approach. It’s not that AI will replace research in art history; it’s more of a support or tool that can give indications,” notes Celio-Scheurer. “At the moment it’s a support, but who knows how far this tool can be developed?”

article_text:
Sacha Baron Cohen has explained why he decided to resurrect his buffoon alter-ego Ali G after more than a decade.

“The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him,” Baron Cohen writes in a cover essay for Time magazine.

“The world he’s returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven’t just lingered—they’ve metastasized. They’re fueled by the greatest propaganda machine in history—social media—and now by its monstrous child, AI.”

The tracksuit-clad character, whose full name is Alistair Graham, returns in “Ali G: Who Iz I?” alongside Morgana Robinson as Julie. Production of the satirical film was shrouded in secrecy. But his return has prompted mixed reactions, with some people voicing their disapproval of Ali G, who has been criticized for his sexism, cultural appropriation and even racism.

At the film’s recent premiere, Baron Cohen – in character as Ali G – was asked by Variety about the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, to which he replied: “The only merger that’s happening tonight is me and Sydney Sweeney’s babylons” – a response that stoked the controversy.

In his essay, Baron Cohen says that’s the point, because the character is a satirical figure designed to expose prejudice.

“I’ve always designed my characters and comedy as vehicles to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity, though I realize not everyone sees them that way,” Baron Cohen writes in Time. “Ali G is a white imbecile—a delusional cultural appropriator—who steals the fashion and lyrics from his favorite gangsta rap and dancehall idols, from Compton to Kingston.”

“The joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment who take him seriously enough to believe that HBO would hire the stupidest man in the world as an interview host. Like a good bouffon, he undermines that establishment—not the culture he loves and borrows from.”

In the piece, the actor and writer referenced the history of satire, from Ancient Greece through to “Monty Python.” “Regardless of the madness, the method is the same: make the audience laugh as hard and as much as possible, while holding up a mirror to reflect back things that aren’t always comfortable to see or warn of trends we’d rather look away from.”

article_text:
Tratta dall’omonima rassegna ideata dall’artista e curatore indipendente Francesco Arena , la rubrica OTHER IDENTITY – Altre forme di identità culturali e pubbliche vuole essere una cartina al tornasole capace di misurare lo stato di una nuova e più attuale grammatica visiva, presentando il lavoro di autori e artisti che operano con i linguaggi della fotografia, del video e della performance, per indagare i temi dell’identità e dell’autorappresentazione. Questa settimana intervistiamo Simona Nobili .

Other Identity: Simona Nobili

Il nostro privato è pubblico e la rappresentazione di noi stessi si modifica e si spettacolarizza continuamente in ogni nostro agire. Qual è la tua rappresentazione di arte?

«La mia rappresentazione di arte nasce da un’urgenza profonda, da un sentire che spesso a parole non riesco ad esprimere. L’arte è un mezzo di espressione e di conoscenza ma deve venire da dentro. La fotografia è per me un amore tardivo, vengo dal teatro dove ho imparato a non mettere in scena me stessa ma ad essere un tramite e portare qualcosa a chi guarda; cerco di fare altrettanto con la fotografia».

Creiamo delle vere e proprie identità di genere che ognuno di noi sceglie in corrispondenza delle caratteristiche che vuole evidenziare, così forniamo tracce. Qual è la tua “identità” nell’arte contemporanea?

«Onestamente non ci ho mai pensato, credo comunque un’identità complessa anche per il mio percorso artistico nel teatro e nel cinema. Il mio lavoro fotografico nasce dall’osservazione della realtà, della città e delle persone che la abitano. Cerco volti che hanno qualcosa da raccontare, sguardi intensi; quello che mi interessa è il mistero e spero che ogni mia immagine custodisca una piccola storia».

Quanto conta per te l’importanza dell’apparenza sociale e pubblica?

«Non ha troppa importanza, il giusto direi. Considero i social come un’opportunità per condividere le mie fotografie e quindi la mia sensibilità».

Il richiamo, il plagio, la riedizione, il ready made dell’iconografia di un’identità legata al passato, al presente e al contemporaneo sono messi costantemente in discussione in una ricerca affannosa di una nuova identificazione del sé, di un nuovo valore di rappresentazione. Qual è il tuo valore di rappresentazione oggi?

«Essere autentici, oggi più che mai, consapevole di essere la summa di tutto ciò che ho letto, visto, studiato».

ll nostro “agire” pubblico, anche con un’opera d’arte, travolge il nostro quotidiano, la nostra vita intima, i nostri sentimenti o, meglio, la riproduzione di tutto ciò che siamo e proviamo ad apparire nei confronti del mondo. Tu ti definisci un’artista agli occhi del mondo?

«Non mi definisco un’artista ma una persona che ha uno sguardo particolare sul mondo».

Quale “identità culturale e pubblica” avresti voluto essere oltre a quella che ti appartiene?

«Nessuna in particolare in questo momento. Essere semplicemente me stessa è già abbastanza complesso ma è anche divertente».

Biografia

Simona Nobili ha scoperto la fotografia parallelamente alla sua carriera di attrice, formandosi all’Istituto Superiore di Cinema e Televisione Roberto Rossellini di Roma, con una specializzazione in fotografia analogica. La sua ricerca visiva si muove tra tecnica digitale e analogica, in un dialogo costante tra tradizione e contemporaneità.

Al centro del suo lavoro ci sono l’identità e la memoria. Il bianco e nero, con i suoi contrasti decisi, diventa il linguaggio ideale per restituire la complessità della condizione umana. Negli ultimi anni le sue fotografie sono state esposte in mostre personali e collettive sia in Italia che all’estero ed è presente con alcune opere nella Mediterraneum Collection.

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这本书的遗产让我着迷了十多年。吉尔马的叙事，以及他不顾风险坚持叙事的决心，为在各种学科和背景下工作的艺术家们提供了礼物和教训，这些背景下创造力可能被视为一种威胁，”埃里克·戈特斯曼表示。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
For Freedoms , an artist-led organization deepening civic engagement by centering artists as essential to shaping a free and pluralist society, presents two new exhibitions marking the third and final year of its three-year artist residency with the Corcoran School of the Arts and Design at the George Washington University. Night and Day , by artist Eric Gottesman , is one of them.

Night and Day centers on Ethiopian journalist and author Baalu Girma’s controversial 1983 Amharic novel Oromay , written under Ethiopia’s Derg regime and banned shortly after its publication. Drawing on artist Eric Gottesman’s longstanding engagement with the novel, the exhibition considers how artists create, communicate, and sustain cultural memory within and against conditions of censorship, political repression, and state violence.

The exhibition’s title comes from Girma’s own divided existence. By day, he worked at his desk writing propaganda for the Derg; by night, at his kitchen table, he wrote fiction in longhand, with pencil and paper. In Oromay , Girma drew on that same duality as a literary strategy, blending fact and fiction and borrowing techniques from Ethiopian poetic traditions like qine to encode political meaning beneath the surface of his prose, saying one thing while also saying another. Oromay stands as both a case study and a blueprint for fiction’s capacity to interrogate power, not only under the Derg, but under oppressive political regimes more broadly.

Since 2011, Gottesman has developed a series of translations, interpretations, and adaptations of Oromay . In 2012, working with Yawoinshet Masresha and Girma’s family, he co-published the first authorized translated excerpt of the novel, and only the second translation of Amharic fiction into English. In the years since, he has collaborated with designers, artists, writers, and filmmakers across Ethiopia, Eritrea, and the United States to translate the novel and the story of its author into new forms, including photography, video installation, collaborative workshops, works on paper, and sculpture.

“The legacy of this single book has obsessed me for over a decade. Girma’s storytelling, and his commitment to it despite the risks, serves as a gift and a lesson to artists working in various disciplines and in contexts where creativity can be seen as a threat,” says Eric Gottesman.

Night and Day asks a question Gottesman considers particularly urgent in the United States today: what can we do with a banned book? Using translation, strategies of doubling, and reciprocal viewing, the exhibition treats Girma’s writing not only as inspiration but, at times, as raw physical material, examining how art can construct what Gottesman calls a politics of possibility. Taken together, the works on view ask what Girma’s writing reveals about the risks artists take to speak freely, in the Ethiopia where he wrote and in the United States today, where freedom of expression is likewise under duress.

The exhibition brings together photography, video, sculpture, and works on paper spanning two decades of Gottesman’s engagement with Oromay . Its title work, Night and Day / ቅነ ጥሬጰዛ, a kinetic sculpture created with designer Jomo Tariku and artist Adiskidan Ambaye, combines plywood, etched acrylic, scrolls of cotton, paper, and thread, pigment prints, and a motion-sensing motor. Baalu Girma’s Portrait , a three-channel video installation, draws on interviews with the author’s wife, Almaz, his daughter, Meskerem Girma, and his best friend, Abiyi Ford, offering a rare, intimate portrait of the man behind the novel. Other works draw directly on the physical object of the book itself: Flag incorporates screenprinting on pages of the banned novel. Additional works include the films Colonel’s Mirror (2017) and Elilta and Fiammeta (2026); My Flesh and My Soul , spanning 2012 to 2026; and Absence (2006), a redacted stack of C-41 photographic prints made in Ethiopian photography studios.

The exhibition includes works made in collaboration with designers, artists, writers, and filmmakers including Jomo Tariku, Daniel Debebe Negatu, Yoni Brook, Adiskidan Ambaye, Tegegn Samuel, and Yawoinshet Masresha, among others.

On view at the Corcoran October 28, 2026 – February 19, 2027
